The parser changes themselves don't have a11y impact. Web developers can already construct arbitrary node trees using API calls and browsers already have to handle those. This is purely about what trees can be constructed using syntax instead of API calls.

Now there is a separate question as to what the new content model of the `select` element is going to be and there we should discuss any new kind of a11y mapping that goes with that and how to determine the fallback for platforms that won't enable the richer rendering, etc.

_Writing this with my TAG hat on, and is the same feedback I would give during a design review._

Requiring an opt-in so that HTML content can work in the predictable, obvious way is author-hostile. Elements being dropped within `<select>` and `<option>` has historically been the source of a lot of author pain, even outside styling use cases (e.g. in scripting). Fixing it by introducing more syntax means the default behavior continues to be unintuitive, while authors need to learn yet another trick so their HTML works in the expected way. Opting to hold up such a confusing behavior to avoid changing how unclosed `<select>`s render in a tiny fraction of obscure websites is …the wrong weighing of priorities IMO. 

Not to mention it makes it impossible to use this feature via progressive enhancement, since it completely breaks `<select>` in browsers that don’t support this. This is not necessarily a showstopper by itself, but it will slow down adoption considerably which also means that by the time we have enough author feedback about using it on real-world scenarios, it will be too late to change it in any way.

It might have been a reasonable weighing of tradeoffs if the use counter showed a much higher percentage, but 0.3% is actually _encouraging_ as an upper bound for breakage. I suspect for many, if not most, cases within that 0.3%, the change will actually _fix_ content that is currently broken. E.g. in the example given of an unclosed `<select>` that is eating up the rest of the page, I’d argue the change actually makes the content _more_ accessible. And as it was pointed out, in many other cases, the content is still _functional_, even if it looks broken.

I think it's really important to emphasize that this issue ("HTML Parser changes for...") is about just the **parser changes**. Allowing all content (a.k.a. "option 1") does **not** necessarily mean all content is fully supported. It means all content is **parsed**. An important point to make, though, is that similar to the web platform, accessibility is not static. FWIW, this goes beyond AT (though keyboards _are_ AT, most non-practitioners think "AT" means screen readers). But what I mean is that this comes down to platform support. As, in the browser _and_ the operating system need to support these things and expose them properly for screen readers (and sure, other AT) to be able to use them. Considering how long the trickle of bugs from SVG integration and `template` integration (and their combination!) has been, I feel uneasy about poking `select` parsing at all. However, I realize that there's enough demand for better styling of `select` that not changing the parsing at all is probably not a practical approach.

Therefore, my preference is explicit opt-in with `button` and `datalist` and particular spec writing care taken to consider how `svg`, `math`, and `template` as descendants of `select` affect coming back through the "in select" and the "in select in table" insertion modes when coming out of SVG and `template` for any reason (including breakout from SVG on particular special names).

> Therefore, my preference is explicit opt-in with button and datalist and particular spec writing care taken to consider how svg, math, and template as descendants of select affect coming back through the "in select" and the "in select in table" insertion modes when coming out of SVG and template for any reason (including breakout from SVG on particular special names).

Thanks for the feedback! This was my preference as well, but most of the feedback I've gotten so far is that we shouldn't require datalist to opt into parser changes, so I'm going to try to see how far I can get doing that in chromium.

I discussed this with @hsivonen today.

- We're ok with Chromium experimenting with option 1 to find out if it's acceptable in terms of web compat. With the use counter being 0.3% we expect there will be some broken sites.
- I think option 1 is best for developer experience over the longer term.
- One of @hsivonen 's concerns is that the parser has various assumptions and a change like this can break assumptions in subtle ways that might be discovered later. I suppose tests [for all interesting cases](https://web-platform-tests.org/writing-tests/making-a-testing-plan.html) could help.
I created a spec PR here, review would be appreciated: https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/10557

Analysis of the [mXSS](https://cure53.de/fp170.pdf) risk with this change:

Current parsers will ignore most tags in `select`, and the new parser will not. This allows for getting different parser state between new and legacy parsers, which can be used for mXSS. For example, see https://software.hixie.ch/utilities/js/live-dom-viewer/saved/13018 (targeting legacy browsers where the sanitizer uses the new parsing, but the other way around is probably also possible).

However, as far as I can tell an mXSS attack still needs something else like a RAWTEXT element to be unfiltered, which is more general and e.g. DOMPurify checks for ([demo showing DOMPurify mitigating this Conclusion: sanitizers need to have general protection against mXSS, and so this change doesn't introduce new mXSS vectors, even though the parsed tree can be very different between new and legacy parsers.

For posterity, I posted an update here: https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/10557#issuecomment-2515300782

We [encountered an issue](https://issues.chromium.org/issues/394337117) while rolling out parser changes because a site was doing this:
```html
<select id=select1></select>
<script>
select1.innerHTML = '<select id=select2><option>option</option></select>';
</script>
```
Before the parser changes, the HTML fragment parsing algorithm would somehow set the parser mode to the "in select" mode, which would make `<select id=select2>` get dropped. With the new parser changes, we ended up with nested `<select>`s getting into the DOM tree which broke the site.

In this case, `<select id=select1>` is the fragment parsing [context element](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#concept-frag-parse-context). It seems that looking up through the stack of open elements (which is how the spec PR tries to prevent nested `<select>`s) does not find the context element, and I also saw the [fragment case](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#fragment-case) note which if I'm reading correctly says that we aren't allowed to change the actual tree building algorithm based on whether we are parsing a fragment.

Can anyone recommend how to change the spec PR to un-break this case?

To follow up on my previous comment:

Here is the line of the existing spec which supports the innerHTML behavior in [reset-the-insertion-mode-appropriately](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#reset-the-insertion-mode-appropriately)

> Loop: If node is the first node in the stack of open elements, then set last to true, and, if the parser was created as part of the [HTML fragment parsing algorithm](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#html-fragment-parsing-algorithm) ([fragment case](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#fragment-case)), set node to the [context](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#concept-frag-parse-context) element passed to that algorithm.

This sets the parser mode to the "in select mode", which is what prevents the nested select element from being parsed.

I added prose like this to the select element case in the parser to fix the regression: https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/10557/commits/9d860113c21b35a2db45be3245784cfa1741260a

Allow any tags inside <select>
(Most flexible, but might break old websites)

Allow only <button> and <datalist> inside <select>
(Safer, but still adds flexibility)

Allow any tags inside <option>, <button>, or <datalist>
(Even more controlled)
